## A Bad Morning {.center}

> "The portfolio was diversified. Low correlations everywhere."
>
> Then one shock arrived — and everything fell at once.

. . .

**What did the number miss?**

That question drives this entire lecture.

## Your Data

In finance you work with:

- **Daily returns** — fat-tailed, volatility-clustered
- **Factor exposures** — linear structure, but the residuals aren't
- **Credit tables** — binary outcomes, group structure

The *joint* behaviour is what matters.  Marginals lie.

## Why It's Hard — The Shapes

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.8
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 350
t = rng.normal(size=n)
x1 = 0.8*t + 0.4*rng.normal(size=n); y1 = 0.8*t + 0.4*rng.normal(size=n)  # linear
x2 = rng.uniform(-2.5,2.5,n); y2 = x2**2 + 0.5*rng.normal(size=n)          # U-shape
x3 = rng.normal(size=n); y3 = rng.normal(size=n)                             # tail crash
crash = rng.random(n) < 0.08
x3[crash] -= rng.uniform(2,4,crash.sum()); y3[crash] -= rng.uniform(2,4,crash.sum())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.8))
titles = ["Linear (Pearson sees this)", "Non-linear (Pearson blind)", "Tail crash (Pearson blind)"]
data = [(x1,y1,COOL,None), (x2,y2,WARM,None), (x3,y3,COOL,crash)]
for ax, (x,y,col,m), title in zip(axes, data, titles):
    if m is None:
        ax.scatter(x, y, s=12, c=col, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
    else:
        ax.scatter(x[~m], y[~m], s=12, c=col, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
        ax.scatter(x[m], y[m], s=20, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## The Running Characters {.center}

We follow **two pairs** down every rung of the ladder.

. . .

**The banks** — strong dependence + joint crashes.
Pearson says "high". The lesson is the extra tail risk it misses.

. . .

**The convex payoff** — $v = |u| + \text{noise}$.
Pearson says "nothing". The ladder's hero case.

## Two Roads to Measure Dependence

There are only **two ways** to ask "how much do these move together?"

. . .

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Road 1 — compare directly**

`compare( T(x), T(y) )` — no density needed

- Pearson
- Spearman
- distance correlation
- HSIC / CKA
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
**Road 2 — through the density**

*how far is the joint from independent, in bits?*

- entropy → mutual information
- total correlation
- Linfoot R
- Gaussianization
:::

::::

. . .

The **transform** $T$ is the thread through both.

---

## Two Roads — Same Data, Both Ways

```{python}
#| echo: false
a, b, _ = datasets.two_banks(n=2000)
ra, rb = rankdata(a), rankdata(b)
fig, (ax0, ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.5, 3.9))
ax0.scatter(a, b, s=8, c=INK, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
ax0.set_title("The data", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
ax1.scatter(ra, rb, s=8, c=COOL, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
ax1.set_title(f"Road 1 · compare transforms\ncorr(rank a, rank b) = {pearsonr(ra, rb)[0]:.2f}",
              fontsize=13)
grid = np.linspace(-4.2, 2.8, 120)
XX, YY = np.meshgrid(grid, grid)
Z = gaussian_kde(np.vstack([a, b]))(np.vstack([XX.ravel(), YY.ravel()])).reshape(XX.shape)
Zind = gaussian_kde(a)(grid)[None, :] * gaussian_kde(b)(grid)[:, None]
ax2.contourf(XX, YY, Z, levels=10, cmap="Oranges")
ax2.contour(XX, YY, Zind, levels=6, colors=COOL, linewidths=1.4)
ax2.set_title(f"Road 2 · through the density\nMI = {mutual_information_xy(a, b) / np.log(2):.2f} bits",
              fontsize=13)
for ax in (ax0, ax1, ax2):
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Road 1 never touches a density — it reshapes the **points** and compares them.
Road 2 fits the **density** (orange) and measures its gap from the independent
version (blue contours) — in **bits**.

---

## Road 1 · Compare Directly {.center}

No density required — **transform** each variable, then measure a **distance**:

`measure = compare( transform(x), transform(y) )`

. . .

Four rungs of increasing reach:
**Pearson → Spearman → distance correlation → HSIC**.

---

## #1 Pearson — The Line

$$r = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\,\sigma_Y} \in [-1, 1]$$

- Measures **linear** co-movement only
- Fast, familiar, the default everywhere

## #2 Spearman — Ranks

$$\rho_S = \operatorname{corr}(\operatorname{rank}(X),\; \operatorname{rank}(Y))$$

Only one slot changes from Pearson — the **transform**:

```
Pearson   = corr( x       , y       )
Spearman  = corr( rank(x) , rank(y) )
```

Catches any *monotonic* relationship.  Fails on U-shapes.

## #2 Spearman — The Transform, Seen

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n = 400
x = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
y = np.exp(0.9 * x) * (1 + 0.18 * rng.normal(size=n))   # compounding payoff
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 3.9))
axL.scatter(x, y, s=12, c=WARM, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
axL.set_title(f"Raw data — compounding payoff\nPearson r = {pearsonr(x, y)[0]:.2f}", fontsize=13)
axR.scatter(rankdata(x), rankdata(y), s=12, c=COOL, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
axR.set_title(f"After the transform — rank(x) vs rank(y)\nPearson on ranks = Spearman = {spearmanr(x, y)[0]:.2f}",
              fontsize=13)
for ax in (axL, axR):
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The payoff compounds, so the relationship bends and Pearson under-reports.
**Ranks straighten the curve** — Spearman *is* Pearson on the right panel.

## #2 Spearman — The Seed

Notice: Pearson and Spearman are the **same move**, different transform.

```
general = compare( transform(x) , transform(y) )
```

. . .

**First road**: compare directly, never needing the distribution.

Plant the seed: *do you need the distribution?*
**No** → stay here. **Yes** → the other road.

---

## Same Correlation, Different Reality

**All four share Pearson ≈ 0.30** — yet each hides a different reality.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
N, TARGET = 600, 0.30

def tune(xx, struct, target, rng):
    s = (struct - struct.mean()) / struct.std()
    ind = rng.normal(0, 1, len(xx)); ind = (ind - ind.mean()) / ind.std()
    best = None
    for w in np.linspace(0.05, 1, 200):
        yy = w * s + (1 - w) * ind
        r = pearsonr(xx, yy)[0]
        if best is None or abs(abs(r) - target) < abs(abs(best[1]) - target):
            best = (yy, r)
    return best

xa = rng.normal(0, 1, N); ya, ra = tune(xa, xa, TARGET, rng)
xb = rng.uniform(-3, 3, N); yb, rb = tune(xb, -(xb**2)+0.9*xb, TARGET, rng)
xc0 = rng.normal(0,1,N); yc0 = rng.normal(0,1,N); rc, crash_c = None, None
for frac in np.linspace(0.04, 0.18, 40):
    m = rng.random(N) < frac
    xx, yy = xc0.copy(), yc0.copy()
    sh = rng.uniform(1.3, 3.2, m.sum())
    xx[m] = -sh + rng.normal(0, .18, m.sum()); yy[m] = -sh + rng.normal(0, .18, m.sum())
    r = pearsonr(xx, yy)[0]
    if rc is None or abs(r - TARGET) < abs(rc - TARGET):
        rc, crash_c, xc, yc = r, m, xx, yy
xd = rng.uniform(-3, 3, N); nd = rng.normal(0, 1, N)
best_d = None
for a in np.linspace(0, 1.3, 220):
    yy = a * xd + nd * (0.25 + 0.7 * np.abs(xd))
    r = pearsonr(xd, yy)[0]
    if best_d is None or abs(r - TARGET) < abs(best_d[1] - TARGET):
        best_d = (yy, r)
yd, rd = best_d

panels = [("Linear", xa, ya, ra, None), ("Curved", xb, yb, rb, None),
          ("Quiet, then crash", xc, yc, rc, crash_c), ("Drift + rising risk", xd, yd, rd, None)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10.5, 6.0))
for ax, (t, x, y, r, mask) in zip(axes.flat, panels):
    if mask is None:
        ax.scatter(x, y, s=22, c=COOL, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
    else:
        ax.scatter(x[~mask], y[~mask], s=22, c=COOL, alpha=0.45, edgecolors="none")
        ax.scatter(x[mask], y[mask], s=34, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(f"{t}    ·    Pearson = {r:+.2f}", fontsize=14)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## #3 Distance Correlation — Any Shape

$$\operatorname{dCor}(X, Y) \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{dCov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{dVar}(X)\,\operatorname{dVar}(Y)}} \;\in\; [0, 1]$$

Same template, a new transform — still **no density**:

```
Pearson  = corr(  x       ,  y       )
dCor     = corr(  dist(x) ,  dist(y) )
```

- $\operatorname{dCov}^2 = \overline{A_{ij}\,B_{ij}}$ — average product of the **centered distances**
- **Zero if and only if independent** — any shape counts

---

## #3 Distance Correlation — The Transform

The transform, seen: one day becomes its **distances to every other day**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
def convex_clean(n=120, noise=0.08, seed=42):
    # the convex pair with the noise turned down, so matrix structure is visible
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    u = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    return u, np.abs(u) + noise * rng.normal(0, 1, n)


u, v = convex_clean()
order = np.argsort(u)
us, vs = u[order], v[order]
A = np.abs(us[:, None] - us[None, :])
B = np.abs(vs[:, None] - vs[None, :])
i = 12  # anchor day, low u
fig, (ax0, ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.5, 3.9))
ax0.scatter(us, vs, s=14, c=WARM, alpha=0.45, edgecolors="none")
ax0.scatter([us[i]], [vs[i]], s=70, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
for j in range(0, len(us), 14):
    ax0.plot([us[i], us[j]], [vs[i], vs[j]], color=GRID, lw=0.8, zorder=1)
ax0.set_title("One day vs every other day", fontsize=13)
despine(ax0)
for ax, M, ttl, cmap in [(ax1, A, "all pairwise distances in X", "Blues"),
                         (ax2, B, "all pairwise distances in Y", "Oranges")]:
    ax.imshow(M, cmap=cmap, origin="lower")
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=13)
    ax.axhline(i, color=CRASH, lw=1.4)
for ax in (ax0, ax1, ax2):
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Days sorted by $x$.  The X-distances form a smooth gradient; the Y-distances show
the V as a **cross** — the structure survives the transform, no density in sight.

---

## #3 Distance Correlation — Then Compare

Then the **same move as always** — Pearson, on the *centered distances*:

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 300
u, v = datasets.convex_payoff(n=n)
xi, yi = rng.normal(size=n), rng.normal(size=n)


def centered_distances(z):
    d = np.abs(z[:, None] - z[None, :])
    return d - d.mean(0) - d.mean(1)[:, None] + d.mean()


sub = rng.choice(n * n, 4000, replace=False)
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 3.9))
for ax, (x, y), name, col in [(axL, (u, v), "Convex pair", WARM),
                              (axR, (xi, yi), "Independent pair", COOL)]:
    Ac, Bc = centered_distances(x).ravel()[sub], centered_distances(y).ravel()[sub]
    ax.scatter(Ac, Bc, s=6, c=col, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\ncorr of centered distances = {pearsonr(Ac, Bc)[0]:.2f}"
                 f"   ·   dCor = {distance_correlation(x, y):.2f}", fontsize=13)
    ax.set_xlabel("centered |xi − xj|", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("centered |yi − yj|", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

That correlation *is* **dCor²** — dependence of any shape becomes a plain
linear trend in distance space.

---

## #4 HSIC — Dependence Without a Density {.center}

$$\operatorname{HSIC}(X, Y) = \frac{1}{(n-1)^2}\operatorname{tr}(K_X H K_Y H)$$

- Zero *exactly* under independence
- No density estimate needed
- **Differentiable** → usable as a training penalty

. . .

The kernel generalization of distance correlation — the most general Road 1 test.
*The same HSIC becomes the fairness penalty in Lecture 2.*

---

## #4 HSIC — In Pictures

Swap *distance* for **kernel similarity**: $K_{ij}$ = how alike days $i$ and $j$ are.

```{python}
#| echo: false
u, v = convex_clean()
order = np.argsort(u)
us, vs = u[order], v[order]


def rbf_gram(z):
    d2 = (z[:, None] - z[None, :]) ** 2
    s = np.sqrt(np.median(d2[d2 > 0]) / 2)
    return np.exp(-d2 / (2 * s * s))


K, L = rbf_gram(us), rbf_gram(vs)
nk = len(us)
H = np.eye(nk) - np.ones((nk, nk)) / nk
agree = (H @ K @ H) * (H @ L @ H)
vmax = np.percentile(np.abs(agree), 98)
fig, (ax0, ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.5, 3.9))
for ax, M, ttl, cmap, kw in [
    (ax0, K, "similar days in X", "Blues", {}),
    (ax1, L, "similar days in Y", "Oranges", {}),
    (ax2, agree, f"where the patterns agree\nCKA = {cka_rbf(u, v):.2f}", "PuOr",
     {"vmin": -vmax, "vmax": vmax}),
]:
    ax.imshow(M, cmap=cmap, origin="lower", **kw)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=13)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

$\operatorname{tr}(K_X H K_Y H)$ just **sums the third panel** — HSIC is large
when the two similarity patterns light up in the same places.

---

## Road 1 · Side by Side

Same two characters, all four rungs.  Each new rung catches what the last missed:

```{python}
#| echo: false

u, v = datasets.convex_payoff(n=500)
methods = ["Pearson", "Spearman", "distance\ncorr", "HSIC"]
banks = [abs(pearsonr(a, b)[0]), abs(spearmanr(a, b)[0]),
         distance_correlation(a, b), cka_rbf(a, b)]
convex = [abs(pearsonr(u, v)[0]), abs(spearmanr(u, v)[0]),
          distance_correlation(u, v), cka_rbf(u, v)]
xs = np.arange(4); wbar = 0.38
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.6))
ax.axvspan(-0.5, 1.5, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
ax.bar(xs - wbar / 2, banks, wbar, color=COOL, label="Banks (a line)")
ax.bar(xs + wbar / 2, convex, wbar, color=WARM, label="Convex (a V)")
ax.set_xticks(xs); ax.set_xticklabels(methods, fontsize=14)
ax.set_ylabel("dependence detected"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.text(0.5, 0.93, "blind to the V", ha="center", fontsize=13, color=CRASH,
        style="italic", fontweight="bold")
ax.text(2.5, 0.93, "sees any shape", ha="center", fontsize=13,
        color=plotting.PALETTE["green"], style="italic", fontweight="bold")
ax.legend(fontsize=12, frameon=False, loc="center right")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Pearson & Spearman collapse on the convex V; distance correlation and HSIC hold.

---

## Road 2 · Through the Density {.center}

A different question: *how far is the joint from independent — in bits?*

That needs the **density** $p(x,y)$ — **assume** its shape (parametric, fast, wrong
in the tails) or **learn** it (Gaussianization).

. . .

**Independence → entropy → MI → total correlation → Linfoot → Gaussianization**

---

## Independence as the Reference

Independent means $p(x, y) = p(x)\,p(y)$.  Shuffle one column and you *build* that
reference: same marginals, all dependence destroyed.  **Dependence = distance from
the shuffled version.**

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 450
x = rng.normal(size=n); y = 0.9 * x + 0.45 * rng.normal(size=n)
y_ref = rng.permutation(y)                      # same values, link destroyed
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 3.6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
axL.scatter(x, y, s=20, c=WARM, alpha=0.55, edgecolors="none")
axL.set_title("The data — dependent", fontsize=14)
axR.scatter(x, y_ref, s=20, c=COOL, alpha=0.55, edgecolors="none")
axR.set_title("Independent reference — Y shuffled", fontsize=14)
for ax in (axL, axR):
    ax.set_xlabel("X"); ax.set_ylabel("Y"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

---

## #5 Entropy — Information Is Surprise

A rare event is **surprising**; a near-certain one tells you almost nothing:

$$I(x) = \log\frac{1}{p(x)}$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
p = np.linspace(0.004, 1.0, 500)
info = np.log2(1.0 / p)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.6))
ax.plot(p, info, color=COOL, lw=3)
for pv, lab, off in [(0.5, "ordinary day\n1 bit", (30, 10)),
                     (0.01, "crash day\n6.6 bits", (40, -8))]:
    ax.scatter([pv], [np.log2(1 / pv)], s=80, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(lab, (pv, np.log2(1 / pv)), textcoords="offset points", xytext=off,
                ha="center", fontsize=12, color=INK)
ax.set_xlabel("P(event)"); ax.set_ylabel("surprise  (bits)")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The rarer the outcome, the more **bits** it carries.

---

## #5 Entropy — The Average Surprise

**Entropy is the *expected* surprise** — how unpredictable a variable is on
average. Volatile returns = high entropy = genuinely harder to predict.

$$H(X) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\log\frac{1}{p(X)}\right] = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
p = np.linspace(0.001, 0.999, 400)
H = -p * np.log2(p) - (1 - p) * np.log2(1 - p)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.9))
ax.plot(p, H, color=COOL, lw=3)
marks = [(0.5, "fair coin\n1 bit", (0, -52)), (0.9, "biased 90/10\n0.47 bit", (-2, 14))]
for pv, lab, off in marks:
    hv = -pv * np.log2(pv) - (1 - pv) * np.log2(1 - pv)
    ax.scatter([pv], [hv], s=80, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(lab, (pv, hv), textcoords="offset points", xytext=off,
                ha="center", fontsize=12, color=INK)
ax.set_xlabel("P(heads)"); ax.set_ylabel("entropy H  (bits)")
ax.set_title("A fair coin is the hardest to predict", fontsize=13)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.15); despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## #5 Entropy — In Pictures

Same question every morning: *what will today's return be?*

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
nE = 6000
bins = np.linspace(-8, 8, 33)


def hist_entropy_bits(s):
    cnt, _ = np.histogram(s, bins=bins)
    prob = cnt / cnt.sum()
    prob = prob[prob > 0]
    return -(prob * np.log2(prob)).sum() + 0.0  # +0.0 avoids displaying "-0.0"


panels = [("Pegged currency", 0.25 + 0.02 * rng.normal(size=nE), COOL),
          ("Calm asset", 0.6 * rng.normal(size=nE), COOL),
          ("Volatile asset", 2.5 * rng.normal(size=nE), WARM)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.4), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, s, col) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.hist(s, bins=bins, density=True, color=col, alpha=0.75)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=13)
    ax.text(0.5, 0.78, f"H = {hist_entropy_bits(s):.1f} bits", transform=ax.transAxes,
            ha="center", fontsize=16, fontweight="bold", color=INK,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.4", fc=PANEL, ec=GRID))
    ax.set_xlabel("daily return")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The wider the distribution, the more average surprise — the more **bits** it takes
to describe a day.

## #6 Mutual Information — In Pictures

Two variables can **share** surprise.  Toy data, the Venn it maps to, and the bits it earns:

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 2500
xd = rng.uniform(-2.5, 2.5, n); yd = xd**2 + 0.5 * rng.normal(size=n)  # dependent (curved)
xi = rng.normal(size=n); yi = rng.normal(size=n)                        # independent

def mi_bits(x, y):
    return mutual_information_bits(np.histogram2d(x, y, bins=10)[0])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.5, 6.0))
gs = GridSpec(2, 2, height_ratios=[1.25, 1], hspace=0.3, wspace=0.18)

# top row — the toy data
axDs = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
axDs.scatter(xd, yd, s=8, c=WARM, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
axDs.set_title("Dependent data (curved)", fontsize=13)
axIs = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
axIs.scatter(xi, yi, s=8, c=COOL, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
axIs.set_title("Independent data", fontsize=13)
for ax in (axDs, axIs):
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)

# bottom row — the Venn it maps to, with MI
def mini_venn(ax, overlap, mi, label):
    ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 6); ax.axis("off"); ax.set_aspect("equal")
    dx = 1.5 if overlap else 2.7
    _venn_circle(ax, (5 - dx, 3), 2.0, COOL)
    _venn_circle(ax, (5 + dx, 3), 2.0, WARM)
    if overlap:
        ax.text(5, 3, "MI", family="monospace", ha="center", va="center",
                fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=INK, zorder=6)
    ax.set_title(f"{label}  →  MI = {mi:.2f} bit", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")

mini_venn(fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0]), True, mi_bits(xd, yd), "overlap")
mini_venn(fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1]), False, mi_bits(xi, yi), "no overlap")
plt.show()
```

---

## #6 Mutual Information — The Honest Measure {.center}

**Shared information = each variable's surprise, minus the surprise of the pair:**

$$I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) \geq 0$$

**Equivalently — the distance from the independent reference:**

$$I(X;Y) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p(x,y)\,\|\,p(x)\,p(y)\big)$$

Zero *only* under independence; positive whenever they share structure.

---

## The Dial · One Value: $H(X)$

So far one sample = one **day** of one series: a single value.  Its uncertainty is **entropy**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# series + a reusable one-row panel (reused on the next two slides)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
T = 26; t = np.arange(T)
common = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 1, T))
x_series = 0.7 * common + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.5, T))
y_series = 0.7 * np.roll(common, 1) + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.5, T))
x_series = (x_series - x_series.mean()) / x_series.std()
y_series = (y_series - y_series.mean()) / y_series.std()


def _dial(highlight=None, second_hl=None, measure="", desc="", mcolor=COOL, two=False):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(11, 3.3))
    gs = GridSpec(1, 2, figure=fig, width_ratios=[1.85, 1], wspace=0.12)
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
    ax.plot(t, x_series, color=COOL, lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=4, label="X")
    if two:
        ax.plot(t, y_series, color=WARM, lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=4, label="Y")
        ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=12, frameon=False, ncol=2)
    y0, y1 = ax.get_ylim()
    if highlight is not None:
        s, w = highlight
        ax.axvspan(s - 0.4, s + w - 0.6, color=COOL, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((s - 0.4, y0), w - 0.2, y1 - y0, boxstyle="round,pad=0",
                                    fill=False, edgecolor=COOL, lw=2.5, zorder=5))
    if second_hl is not None:
        s, w = second_hl
        ax.axvspan(s - 0.4, s + w - 0.6, color=WARM, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((s - 0.4, y0), w - 0.2, y1 - y0, boxstyle="round,pad=0",
                                    fill=False, edgecolor=WARM, lw=2.5, zorder=5))
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_xlabel("time (trading days) →", fontsize=13, color="#555")
    ax.set_ylabel("return", fontsize=13, color="#555")
    for sp in ax.spines.values():
        sp.set_edgecolor(GRID)
    axR = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1]); axR.axis("off")
    axR.text(0.5, 0.66, desc, ha="center", fontsize=14, color="#555")
    axR.text(0.5, 0.28, measure, family="monospace", ha="center", fontsize=26,
             fontweight="bold", color=mcolor, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.45", fc=PANEL, ec=GRID))
    plt.show()


_dial(highlight=(8, 1), measure="H(X)", desc="uncertainty of one value")
```

One value per day → $H(X)$, the surprise of a single variable.

      mcolor="#7d6b8f", two=True)

Shared surprise between two single values → $I(X;Y)$, mutual information.

## All the Measures — One Grid

Two knobs index every measure: **window width**, and **within vs between**.

|  | **WITHIN** one variable | **BETWEEN** two variables |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **one value** | $H(X)$ — entropy | $I(X;Y)$ — mutual information |
| **a window** | $T(\mathbf{x})$ — total correlation | $I(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{y})$ — mutual information |

One family — the dial picks which.

## #7 Linfoot R — MI on the Correlation Scale

$$R = \sqrt{1 - e^{-2\,I}} \in [0, 1]$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
a, b, _ = datasets.two_banks(n=2000)
mi_banks = mutual_information_xy(a, b) / np.log(2)
R_banks = linfoot_r(mi_banks * np.log(2))
mi_axis = np.linspace(0, 3, 300)
R_curve = np.sqrt(1 - np.exp(-2 * mi_axis * np.log(2)))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 2.7))
ax.plot(mi_axis, R_curve, color=COOL, lw=3)
ax.scatter([mi_banks], [R_banks], s=90, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(f"the banks: {mi_banks:.1f} bits  →  R = {R_banks:.2f}",
            (mi_banks, R_banks), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(20, -16),
            fontsize=13, color=INK)
ax.set_xlabel("mutual information  (bits)"); ax.set_ylabel("Linfoot R")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05); despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Bits map onto the familiar $[0, 1]$ axis — and for a Gaussian pair, $R = |\rho|$ **exactly**.

---

## The Gaussian Shadow

> **Correlation is the shadow that mutual information casts when the world is Gaussian.**

```{python}
#| echo: false
a, b, _ = datasets.two_banks(n=800)
u, v = datasets.convex_payoff(n=800)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 3.7))
for ax, x, y, col, name in [(axes[0], a, b, COOL, "Banks — a Gaussian-ish world"),
                            (axes[1], u, v, WARM, "Convex — not Gaussian at all")]:
    X = np.column_stack([x, y])
    gpts = np.linspace(X.min() - 0.5, X.max() + 0.5, 160)
    XX, YY = np.meshgrid(gpts, gpts)
    Z = multivariate_normal(X.mean(0), np.cov(X.T)).pdf(np.dstack([XX, YY]))
    r = pearsonr(x, y)[0]
    R = linfoot_r(mutual_information_xy(x, y))
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=10, c=col, alpha=0.45, edgecolors="none")
    ax.contour(XX, YY, Z, levels=6, colors=INK, linewidths=1.1, alpha=0.65)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nshadow r = {r:+.2f}   ·   information R = {R:.2f}", fontsize=13)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Contours: the Gaussian fitted to each pair.  When the world isn't Gaussian the shadow
loses almost everything — to recover it you must **learn the density**.

---

## #8 Gaussianization — Watch It Work

```{python}
#| echo: false
uG, vG = datasets.convex_payoff(n=1200, seed=0)
XG = np.column_stack([uG, vG])
XG = (XG - XG.mean(0)) / XG.std(0)


def gauss_marginals(D):
    return np.column_stack([gaussianize_1d(D[:, 0]), gaussianize_1d(D[:, 1])])


def rotate(D, deg):
    th = np.deg2rad(deg)
    Rm = np.array([[np.cos(th), -np.sin(th)], [np.sin(th), np.cos(th)]])
    return D @ Rm.T


rngG = np.random.default_rng(0)
P2 = gauss_marginals(XG)
P3 = gauss_marginals(rotate(P2, 45))
P4 = P3
for _ in range(25):
    P4 = gauss_marginals(rotate(P4, rngG.uniform(20, 70)))
mi0 = mutual_information_xy(XG[:, 0], XG[:, 1]) / np.log(2)
mi1 = mutual_information_xy(P4[:, 0], P4[:, 1]) / np.log(2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11.5, 3.3))
for ax, (t, Dk) in zip(axes, [(f"the data — a V\nMI = {mi0:.2f} bits", XG),
                              ("reshape marginals\n(still a V)", P2),
                              ("rotate, reshape again", P3),
                              (f"…repeat → a Gaussian ball\nMI = {mi1:.2f} bits", P4)]):
    ax.scatter(Dk[:, 0], Dk[:, 1], s=6, c=WARM, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(t, fontsize=11); ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Reshape each marginal to Gaussian, **rotate, repeat** — the V melts into a round ball,
and the bits that vanish are exactly the dependence.

---

## #8 Gaussianization — Learn the Density

Iteratively reshape each marginal to Gaussian, rotate to mix residual
dependence, repeat until the joint *is* a standard Gaussian.

. . .

Every step is invertible → exact log-likelihoods.

**The dependence it must remove IS the data's total correlation.**

. . .

*The same machine, run backward in Lecture 3, generates scenarios.*

---

## The Synthesis — Two Roads

**Do you need the whole distribution?**

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="47%"}
**No → compare directly.**

Transform each variable, then compare the transforms — never touching a density.

*Pearson · Spearman · distance correlation · HSIC — they differ only in the transform.*
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
**Yes → go through the density.**

Measure how far the joint sits from independence — in **bits**.

*Assume the shape — parametric: fast, wrong in the tails.*

*Learn the shape — Gaussianization, flows: exact.*
:::

::::

Either way, the **transform** is the thread.

---

## Every Rung, Both Characters

Both roads, one verdict — the full ladder on our two characters:

```{python}
#| echo: false
a, b, _ = datasets.two_banks(n=800)
u, v = datasets.convex_payoff(n=800)


def linf(x, y):
    mb = mutual_information_bits(np.histogram2d(x, y, bins=20)[0])
    return linfoot_r(mb * np.log(2))  # bits → nats → Linfoot R on [0,1]


methods = ["Pearson", "Spearman", "distance\ncorr", "HSIC", "MI\n(Linfoot)"]
banks = [abs(pearsonr(a, b)[0]), abs(spearmanr(a, b)[0]),
         distance_correlation(a, b), cka_rbf(a, b), linf(a, b)]
convex = [abs(pearsonr(u, v)[0]), abs(spearmanr(u, v)[0]),
          distance_correlation(u, v), cka_rbf(u, v), linf(u, v)]
xs = np.arange(5); wbar = 0.38
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.7))
ax.axvspan(-0.5, 1.5, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
ax.axvline(3.5, color=GRID, lw=1.6, ls="--")
ax.bar(xs - wbar / 2, banks, wbar, color=COOL, label="Banks (a line)")
ax.bar(xs + wbar / 2, convex, wbar, color=WARM, label="Convex (a V)")
ax.text(1.5, 1.07, "Road 1 · no density", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(4.0, 1.07, "Road 2 · information", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(0.5, 0.9, "blind to the V", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=CRASH,
        style="italic", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xticks(xs); ax.set_xticklabels(methods, fontsize=13)
ax.set_ylabel("dependence detected"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.15)
ax.legend(fontsize=12, frameon=False, loc="center right")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Pearson & Spearman go blind on the convex V; distance correlation, HSIC, **and MI
all catch it** — the two roads agree.

---

## Which Road, When?

They **agree on detection** — but hand you different things.

| | **Kernel score** · HSIC, dCor, CKA | **Gaussianization** · RBIG, flows |
|---|---|---|
| Gives you | a number: *how much* | the whole density / map |
| Units | kernel-dependent score | **bits** (+ Linfoot R) |
| Cost & data | cheap, one-shot | iterative, data-hungry |
| Invertible? | no | **yes** → generate, propagate |

---

## Which Road, When? {.center}

The **shortcut** (a score) answers *is there dependence?*

. . .

The **exact map** (a density) lets you *use* it — generate, propagate,
neutralize.

---

## The Punchline → Lab {.center}

The same ladder, now on **real S&P 500 returns**.

. . .

JPMorgan & Bank of America share ~0.7 bits of information.

They fall into their worst days together **~7× more often** than
independence allows.

. . .

*That is the dependence correlation cannot see — and the one that actually
threatens a portfolio.*
